segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
Welcome to Psalm Nights. [pause 3]

Let your body be heavy. Let your hands rest. [pause 6]

Tonight's psalm is Psalm 90. Its heading calls it a prayer of Moses. It is the oldest voice in the Psalms, and it speaks about time. Our short days, and God who is from everlasting to everlasting. [pause 5]

We will read it twice. [pause 8]

verses.text: A Prayer of Moses the man of God. Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations.
Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.
Thou turnest man to destruction; and sayest, Return, ye children of men.
For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night.
Thou carriest them away as with a flood; they are as a sleep: in the morning they are like grass which groweth up.
In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth.
For we are consumed by thine anger, and by thy wrath are we troubled.
Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, our secret sins in the light of thy countenance.
For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a tale that is told.
The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away.
Who knoweth the power of thine anger? even according to thy fear, so is thy wrath.
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
Our dwelling place, in every generation. Before your grandparents. Before their grandparents. God has been home to his people all along. [pause 6]

A thousand years to God are like yesterday, like a watch in the night. A watch in the night. To God, all of history is like a few hours of the dark. [pause 8]

The psalm is honest about how short life is. Like grass in the morning, gone by evening. And so it asks for wisdom. Teach us to number our days. [pause 8]

Two more lines from the end of the psalm. [pause 4]

verses.text: O satisfy us early with thy mercy; that we may rejoice and be glad all our days.
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
Satisfy us early with thy mercy. A prayer for the morning. [pause 6]

And establish the work of our hands. Whatever you did today, small or large, you can ask God to make it count. [pause 8]

Here is Psalm 90 again. Let the long time of God hold your short night. [pause 10]

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text:
Now let the words go quiet. [pause 8]

You do not have to hold on to them. They will be there in the morning. [pause 10]

Let your shoulders drop. Let your hands open. Let the bed hold the weight of you. [pause 12]

If a worry comes back, you can hand it over again. As many times as it takes. [pause 12]

The night is long and quiet, and you are not alone in it. [pause 15]

Feel the quiet of the room. The small sounds. The dark. Nothing is asked of you here. [pause 20]

You are held, the psalm said. You are known. You are kept. [pause 20]

Rest now. [pause 45]

first_reader.note: Written by Claude in the landing session, then Claude's pastor and cultural read.

pastor.note: Stored KJV pasted by code; short echoes only. Each night keeps its psalm's own point (contentment, tasting God's goodness, remembering benefits, night watches, honest sadness, the higher rock, longing for God's house, our short days, return to rest, surrounded like Jerusalem). Psalm 103's 'healeth' told as memory of who God has been, not a promise; Psalm 42 points a long sadness to a pastor, a doctor or a friend; no sleep or safety promise in the new rests.

cultural.note: Plain English for a tired listener; grief and low nights named without pity; two new shared rests so closes vary; pacing by silence only (13.6-15.1 min).
